sources.title: Being Realistic about Reasons: John Locke Lectures 4 and 5
sources.author: T. M. Scanlon
sources.locator: Lecture 4, pp. 1–3, 13–20 and 24–26; Lecture 5, pp. 15–21
sources.access: Official Oxford-hosted full lecture PDFs available; selected sections inspected in pass003
sources.note: Distinguishes construction of interpersonal right and wrong from prior reasons, and epistemic justification from normative grounding; Lecture 5 examines contextual comparisons of reasons.
sources.limits: These are 2009 lectures, not the revised 2014 book. Selected passages do not provide a complete theory of conflicting claims or settle the prior-reasons objection.

sources.title: Wrongness and Reasons: A Re-examination
sources.author: T. M. Scanlon
sources.kind: Primary philosophy: chapter in publisher preview
sources.locator: Oxford Studies in Metaethics, volume 2, pp. 5–20; especially pp. 7–11 and 16–18
sources.access: Full chapter present in publisher/distributor preview; selected passages inspected in pass003
sources.note: Reconsiders wrongness and reasons; treats contractualism as an account of an interpersonal form of wrongness rather than every possible moral ground.
sources.limits: MORARG owns its stronger constitutive proposal. This preview includes only the opening page of the following Enoch chapter and does not establish that chapter was read.

sources.title: Agency, Shmagency: Why Normativity Won’t Come from What Is Constitutive of Action
sources.author: David Enoch
sources.kind: Primary philosophy: journal text through public mirror
sources.locator: The Philosophical Review 115(2), 169–198; §3, pp. 177–180; discussion of inescapability; §§7–8, pp. 192–196
sources.access: Selected primary text inspected through an indexed public mirror; title and publication checked against author records; publisher PDF not retrieved
sources.note: Constitutive features of agency do not by themselves establish their authority; the later epistemic appeal to deliberative indispensability is a separate argument.
sources.limits: Mirror OCR can contain errors. This is a selected-argument review, not a full reading of Taking Morality Seriously or all replies to constitutivism.

sources.title: Can There Be a Global, Interesting, Coherent Constructivism about Practical Reason?
sources.author: David Enoch
sources.kind: Primary philosophy: manuscript through public mirror
sources.locator: Philosophical Explorations 12(3), 319–339; manuscript §§2.1–2.3, 4.1 and 5 (draft pp. 5–9, 16–18 and 27–36)
sources.access: Selected sections of a full indexed primary manuscript inspected; journal metadata and DOI verified at Hebrew University
sources.note: Distinguishes discovery procedures from constitutive ones, and local construction from a global account of practical reasons; challenges the latter’s deliberative resources.
sources.limits: The accessed text is a draft, not a line-by-line comparison with the final publication. A local interpersonal account avoids the global target only by openly defending its remaining normative premises.

sources.title: Kantian Constructivism in Moral Theory
sources.author: John Rawls
sources.kind: Primary philosophy: journal text through public mirror
sources.locator: The Journal of Philosophy 77(9), 515–572; pp. 516–519, 528–530 and selected passages of Lecture III, especially pp. 565–569
sources.access: Selected primary-text OCR passages inspected in pass003; JSTOR publication record checked
sources.note: Person-conceptions and reasonable constraints shape a construction; the reasonable is not reduced to individual advantage.
sources.limits: Rawls frames justice as fairness for democratic public culture. This is not a general proof of MORARG’s metaethics, nor a complete review of Rawls’s later political liberalism.

sources.title: Moral Realism
sources.author: Peter Railton
sources.locator: The Philosophical Review 95(2), 163–207; especially pp. 164–176 and 189–198
sources.access: Full primary article retrieved; selected sections on objectivity, informed interests and social rationality inspected in pass002
sources.note: A naturalist, relational account that permits criticism of actual approval.
sources.limits: Selected-section review, not an exhaustive assessment. The natural basis of interests must not be confused with approval creating the truth.

sources.title: A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value
sources.author: Sharon Street
sources.locator: Philosophical Studies 127, 109–166; §§1–3, 5–7; pass003 adds §5, pp. 123–124 and §10, pp. 152–155
sources.access: Full primary article retrieved; selected sections inspected in pass002; reflective-equilibrium and concluding antirealist passages inspected in pass003
sources.note: Challenges evolutionary reliability and sketches how actual evaluative error can survive an account grounded in a wider system of attitudes.
sources.limits: Evolutionary causes alone do not refute realism. The concluding sketch is not a full defence of one constructivism and does not itself establish MORARG’s equal-standing premise.

sources.title: Contractualism and Utilitarianism
sources.author: T. M. Scanlon
sources.locator: In Utilitarianism and Beyond, pp. 103–128; indexed opening discussion of justification and moral theory
sources.access: Selected indexed primary passages inspected in pass002; scanned PDF retrieved but text extraction was empty
sources.note: A primary route into interpersonal justification and its substantive moral background.
sources.limits: Not a full-book review. MORARG develops its own constructive proposal; Scanlon’s contractualism alone does not establish antirealism.

sources.title: Being Realistic about Reasons
sources.author: T. M. Scanlon
sources.kind: Primary work: author and publisher synopsis
sources.locator: Book abstract and contents; Harvard author abstract; preview preface describing revision of the lectures
sources.access: Publisher and author abstracts inspected; preview preface checked in pass003; full book not read
sources.note: Defends irreducible normative truths and a role for reflective equilibrium.
sources.limits: The 2009 lectures have a separate entry: the 2014 preface reports substantial revision, so their selected passages cannot be passed off as a full review of this book. Normative cognitivism is not interchangeable with Enoch’s robust realism.

sources.title: Taking Morality Seriously: A Defense of Robust Realism
sources.author: David Enoch
sources.locator: Book abstract and contents; chapters 2–3 on objectivity and deliberative indispensability
sources.access: Publisher abstract and contents inspected in pass002; full book not read
sources.note: An explicit robust realist case takes objective normative reasons seriously in deliberation.
sources.limits: The complete positive argument and replies remain deeper reading. Joyce’s critique is read as a critic, not substituted for Enoch’s own book.

sources.title: Error Theory
sources.author: Richard Joyce
sources.kind: Primary philosophy by an error theorist
sources.locator: International Encyclopedia of Ethics entry; author manuscript, pp. 1–3 and pp. 6–7 on conceptual and ontological premises
sources.access: Author-hosted manuscript retrieved; selected conceptual and practical distinctions inspected in pass002
sources.note: Moral error theory denies moral properties, rather than granting that everything is morally permissible.
sources.limits: Error theory, antirealism and indifference are distinct. The author site labels papers generally as drafts; consult the publication for the definitive text.

sources.title: Taking Moral Skepticism Seriously
sources.author: Richard Joyce
sources.locator: Philosophical Studies 168, 843–851; author manuscript pp. 2–6
sources.access: Author-hosted symposium manuscript retrieved; argument about deliberation, construction and skepticism inspected in pass002
sources.note: Questions whether taking deliberation seriously establishes robust realism rather than another account of reasons.
sources.limits: A substantive critic’s argument, not a neutral verdict on Enoch or proof of error theory.

sources.title: What Is Constructivism in Ethics and Metaethics?
sources.author: Sharon Street
sources.locator: Philosophy Compass 5(5), 363–384; author abstract
sources.access: Publisher abstract and bibliographic record inspected in pass002; full article not reviewed
sources.note: Distinguishes constructivism as a substantive or metaethical position and questions a simple procedural characterisation.
sources.limits: MORARG’s interpersonal proposal is not attributed to Street as her own theory. A fuller comparison with her practical-standpoint view remains open.

sources.title: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III
sources.author: David Hume
sources.access: Selected primary passages inspected in pass001; retained scope in pass002
sources.note: The transition from descriptive premises to moral demands needs an account.
sources.limits: This observation does not itself refute a defended naturalist identity theory.

sources.title: Justice as Fairness: Political, Not Metaphysical
sources.author: John Rawls
sources.locator: Political conception and overlapping-consensus excerpts
sources.access: Primary excerpts inspected in pass001; full article not newly reviewed in pass002
sources.note: Shared political commitments can be pursued amid deeper disagreement.
sources.limits: This is a political account, not a complete antirealist theory of morality.

sources.title: The Belmont Report
sources.author: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research
sources.locator: Part B §§1–3; Part C, informed consent, risk–benefit assessment and selection of subjects
sources.access: Official full text retrieved; principles and application sections inspected in pass002
sources.note: Makes agency, protection, risk and distribution explicit in the ethics of research.
sources.limits: An ethical framework, not empirical proof of its own premises. Official or legal status does not establish moral truth.

sources.title: The Untreated Syphilis Study at Tuskegee Timeline
sources.author: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Background; treatment spotlight; 1972 to present; page dated 4 September 2024
sources.access: Official full page inspected in pass002
sources.note: Documents missing informed consent and withheld treatment in the USPHS study.
sources.limits: A current institutional historical account, not an independent examination of all original records. Modern decision scenarios in MORARG are explicitly hypothetical.

sources.title: Incarceration, Recidivism, and Employment
sources.author: Manudeep Bhuller, Gordon B. Dahl, Katrine V. Løken and Magne Mogstad
sources.locator: Journal of Political Economy 128(4), 1269–1324; author manuscript dated 11 February 2019, §§2–3, 5–6 and 8
sources.access: Author-hosted 92-page manuscript retrieved; selected design, local-effect interpretation, results and limitations inspected; 2020 journal abstract cross-checked
sources.note: Estimates effects of incarceration in Norway using judge stringency; results vary by prior employment.
sources.limits: Identifying assumptions and local population matter. No independent replication. Does not isolate one rehabilitation programme, estimate longer-sentence effects, or warrant direct transfer to every prison system.

sources.title: Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion: 2022 — Executive Summary
sources.author: World Meteorological Organization and the Scientific Assessment Panel
sources.locator: Highlights 1–2; Executive Summary §3, stratospheric ozone; conditional future evolution
sources.access: Official executive-summary text inspected in pass002, including regional qualifications and conditional projections
sources.note: Reports progress in ozone recovery and falling controlled substances, with incomplete and regionally varied recovery.
sources.limits: A dated scientific assessment, not live monitoring or a moral finding. Projections depend on assumptions and compliance; near-global total-column recovery had limited evidence and low confidence.

sources.title: Montreal Protocol, Article 10: Financial mechanism
sources.author: Parties to the Montreal Protocol; text hosted by the UNEP Ozone Secretariat
sources.locator: Current consolidated Article 10, especially paragraphs 1–3, 6 and 9
sources.access: Official consolidated article inspected in pass002; 1990 denotes introduction of the mechanism, not the date of every later amendment
sources.note: An actual mechanism for financial and technical cooperation, including a Multilateral Fund.
sources.limits: The text establishes institutional arrangements. It does not prove their fairness, implementation success, or moral authority.

sources.title: The Emotional Dog and Its Rational Tail
sources.author: Jonathan Haidt
sources.locator: Abstract; Psychological Review 108(4), 814–834
sources.access: Abstract and metadata inspected in pass001; full article not newly reviewed
sources.note: A model of intuitive and social influences on moral judgment.
sources.limits: Used as a limited background source, not a finding that emotion discredits reason or reasoning never changes judgment.

sources.title: Is It Good to Cooperate? Testing the Theory of Morality-as-Cooperation in 60 Societies
sources.author: Oliver Scott Curry, Daniel Austin Mullins and Harvey Whitehouse
sources.locator: Abstract, methods, results and discussion
sources.access: Selected full-text sections inspected in pass001; retained as further reading
sources.note: Cross-cultural patterns in judgments of cooperation.
sources.limits: Coding and coverage constrain generalisation; approval is not moral authority.

sources.title: The Weirdest People in the World?
sources.author: Joseph Henrich, Steven J. Heine and Ara Norenzayan
sources.locator: Abstract; Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33(2–3), 61–83
sources.access: Abstract and author publication metadata inspected in pass001; retained as further reading
sources.note: Sample composition constrains claims about humanity.
sources.limits: A sampling critique does not select a metaethics.

sources.title: Moral Realism
sources.author: Geoff Sayre-McCord
sources.locator: Introduction; §§1, 3, 5
sources.access: Selected sections inspected in pass001; primary realism sources added in pass002
sources.note: An entry point to varied realist commitments.
sources.limits: A scholarly map, not empirical proof or a replacement for the authors’ arguments.

sources.title: Moral Relativism
sources.author: Chris Gowans
sources.access: Selected sections inspected in pass001
sources.note: Distinguishes cultural diversity, relative truth and tolerance.
sources.limits: Not all contextual or informed-attitude accounts reduce to actual approval.

sources.title: Constructivism in Metaethics
sources.author: Carla Bagnoli
sources.locator: Introduction; §§1–3, 5–6
sources.access: Selected sections inspected in pass001; introduction cross-checked in pass002
sources.note: Construction differs from actual consensus; varieties disagree about authority and scope.
sources.limits: MORARG’s specific interpersonal proposal is an authored position, not a claim that all constructivists accept it.

sources.title: Contractualism
sources.author: Elizabeth Ashford and Tim Mulgan
sources.access: Selected sections inspected in pass001
sources.note: Reasonable rejection differs from an actual preference veto.
sources.limits: Contractualism does not by itself entail antirealism.

sources.title: Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism
sources.author: Mark van Roojen
sources.access: Selected sections inspected in pass001
sources.note: Expressivism differs from attitude-reporting subjectivism and error theory.
sources.limits: A short classification is not an exhaustive evaluation of these theories.

sources.title: Monkeys reject unequal pay
sources.author: Sarah F. Brosnan and Frans B. M. de Waal
sources.locator: Nature 425, 297–299; experiment and controls
sources.access: Primary article PDF indexed and selected abstract and methods inspected
sources.note: Reported capuchin refusals under unequal reward conditions.
sources.limits: The interpretation as inequity aversion is contested by later reanalysis and alternative explanations.

sources.title: No evidence for inequity aversion in non-human animals: a meta-analysis of accept/reject paradigms
sources.author: Oded Ritov, Christoph J. Völter, Nichola J. Raihani and Jan M. Engelmann
sources.locator: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 291, 20241452; individual-participant data, 23 studies and 18 species
sources.access: Indexed primary full text and abstract inspected; PMC page returned an access challenge on this pass
sources.note: Reports no statistically clear pooled evidence of inequity aversion in studied accept/reject tasks.
sources.limits: A null result is not proof of no effect or no capacity in all paradigms; samples and available data limit inference.

sources.title: Capuchin monkeys’ responses to inequity in a group context
sources.author: Mayte Martínez and Sarah F. Brosnan
sources.locator: Animal Behaviour 226, 123257; abstract and indexed discussion excerpts
sources.access: Publisher abstract and selected indexed snippets inspected; full paper not reviewed
sources.note: Reports refusals of low-value rewards under disadvantageous inequity, with separate contrast and advantageous-inequity responses in a group setting.
sources.limits: Food value and contrast affect interpretation; number of trades did not depend on the partner’s reward. No independent reanalysis.

sources.title: Chimpanzees’ responses to inequity in a group context are influenced by food quality and their relationships with the group members present
sources.author: Mayte Martínez and colleagues
sources.locator: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 293, 20260397; selected §§2–4, design, measures and discussion
sources.access: Pass003: selected methods, results and discussion inspected in publisher-provided full text hosted on ResearchGate; no data reanalysis
sources.note: Reports context-sensitive responses in a group of chimpanzees.
sources.limits: Voluntary participation in six captive groups; affiliation is not experimentally assigned. Advantageous refusals were too rare for statistical analysis. These measures do not establish a justice concept.

sources.title: No Response to Inconsistently Experienced Inequity in Four Primate Species
sources.author: Simmons and colleagues
sources.locator: American Journal of Primatology; DOI 10.1002/ajp.70196; abstract
sources.access: Publisher and PubMed primary-study abstracts inspected; full text not reviewed
sources.note: At 25% or 50% unequal trials the studied primates did not increase refusals relative to controls.
sources.limits: Null refusal effects do not establish absence of noticing or other responses; task frequency and measures matter.

sources.title: Infants’ Social Evaluation of Helpers and Hinderers: A Large-Scale, Multi-Lab, Coordinated Replication Study
sources.author: Kelsey Lucca, Francis Yuen, Yiyi Wang and colleagues
sources.locator: Developmental Science 28, e13581; abstract; correction DOI 10.1111/desc.70029
sources.access: Primary abstract and indexed methods inspected; published correction inspected by Terra; no independent reanalysis
sources.note: A large coordinated hill-task replication found no above-chance helper preference.
sources.limits: 567 included infants aged 5.5–10.5 months; this task is not a test of all moral capacities. The 2025 correction changes an exploratory analysis, with conclusions unchanged.

sources.title: Infants use helping to infer the existence and strength of caring relationships
sources.author: Bill Pepe, Brandon Woo, Ashley J. Thomas and Lindsey J. Powell
sources.locator: PNAS 123, e2531771123; abstract, four preregistered experiments
sources.access: Primary abstract and selected indexed methods/results inspected; full independent assessment not completed
sources.note: Looking-time findings in 14–15-month-olds suggest relationship-specific expectations about helping.
sources.limits: An indirect measure at a different age, not a direct replication of the hill-choice task; it establishes neither innateness nor moral authority.

sources.title: Bonobos respond aversively to unequal reward distributions
sources.author: Kia Radovanović and colleagues
sources.locator: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 292, 20242873; §§2–4, subjects, controls, results and limitations
sources.access: Primary full-text indexed methods/results/discussion inspected in pass003; no independent reanalysis
sources.note: Two bonobo studies report unequal-reward responses; a human/machine manipulation challenges the social-disappointment explanation.
sources.limits: Six newly tested bonobos in one group; one analysis pooled an older sample. Study 2 was only partly consistent with inequity aversion; partner variation and task constraints limit generalisation.
